name: Cross-Lingual Discovery
title: Cross-Lingual Discovery
answer: Cross-lingual discovery is the practice of finding and producing relevant material in a legal matter when the documents, chats, and audio are not all in one language. It covers the whole pipeline from identifying custodians and sources in several jurisdictions through search, review, and production, and it sits inside e-discovery and large-scale document analysis rather than inside translation as a standalone service. The work is common in matters with operations in the European Union, Asia, or Latin America, where a single custodian may hold records in three or four languages at once.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Cross-lingual discovery is the practice of finding and producing relevant material in a legal matter when the documents, chats, and audio are not all in one language. It covers the whole pipeline from identifying custodians and sources in several jurisdictions through search, review, and production, and it sits inside e-discovery and large-scale document analysis rather than inside translation as a standalone service. The work is common in matters with operations in the European Union, Asia, or Latin America, where a single custodian may hold records in three or four languages at once.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is usually a review platform with multilingual ingestion, optical character recognition for scanned pages, and machine translation or multilingual language models layered on top. Search runs against either translated text or a shared multilingual embedding space, and both approaches are now common in commercial e-discovery tools. Storage and processing are typically cloud hosted, which raises data residency questions when documents originate in jurisdictions with transfer restrictions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with language identification across the corpus, then decide what to translate and what to search natively. Query terms are expanded with synonyms and transliterations, and names are handled carefully because the same person may appear under several romanizations. Review is often tiered, with machine translation used for triage and human translators or bilingual reviewers brought in for documents that will be produced or used in argument. Sampling and quality checks on translated output are standard, because translation errors can hide or invent responsiveness.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters more here than in monolingual review, since a produced document may exist in an original language, a machine translation, and a human translation, and the record should show which was used and when. Privilege and privacy rules differ by jurisdiction, and material that is ordinary business data in one country may be protected personal data in another.Any use of machine translation in a matter should be documented so that opposing counsel and the court can see the method.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Multilingual models are improving fast enough that native-language search is starting to replace translate-then-search as the default. That shift reduces some translation risk but moves the quality question into the model itself, where evaluation is harder and less standardized. Expect more scrutiny of how multilingual systems are validated, and more matters where the language mix is the central technical problem rather than an afterthought.
